frames.narration: A producer offers 1 item per tick. Three consumers take 1.5 per tick, so they keep up: the queue holds at most 1 item and acts as a small buffer.
Now the producer offers 2 per tick for 60 ticks, more than the consumers can take. The difference, half an item per tick, has nowhere to go but the queue.
With an unbounded queue nothing says no. It reaches 31 items and the longest wait is 21 ticks. No error is raised, and memory use just keeps rising with the backlog.

Bound the queue to 10 and block the producer when it is full. The queue stops at 10, the longest wait falls to 7 ticks, and nothing is lost. The producer is held up, and the slowdown travels upstream: this is backpressure.

Or drop instead of blocking. Dropping the newest keeps what is queued and refuses new items; dropping the oldest keeps the freshest. Either way 21 items are lost, which is only fine if the work can be lost or redone.

A bound that is too small backfires. With a limit of 1 the producer and consumers move in lockstep and the consumers are starved: they get only 1 item per tick, and the run takes 123 ticks instead of 83.

The trap: a failed item is put back on the same bounded, blocking queue. When the queue is full and every consumer holds a failed item to put back, nobody can take an item out. The pipeline deadlocks at tick 28 with no error.
